source.title: Among Us: A Sandbox for Measuring and Detecting Agentic Deception

page_placements.theme: SAE feature directions as steering and causal handles (mixed)

record.tranche_reason: The paper evaluates SAE features for deception detection and steering, but does not test feature splitting, dictionary size, or the other listed claim versions.
record.gate_note: No experiments measure whether larger dictionaries replace coarse features with finer ones, whether their inputs partition, or whether their directions form hierarchical families. The SAE detection and steering results concern related feature behavior, not those predictions.
record.test_reason: The paper uses pre-trained Goodfire SAE features for deception detection and steering in an Among Us sandbox. It cites Towards Monosemanticity only as background. It never varies dictionary size, studies feature families, absorption, or training objectives, so no result bears on any feature-splitting version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct but incomplete. The paper's main conclusions are that frontier and RL-trained reasoning models are differentially better at deception than at detection (Deception Elo), and that linear probes trained off-distribution detect deception with AUROCs around 0.95–0.99. The SAE part (two features detect deception well; steering fails) is a minor result.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses SAE features for deception detection and steering, not to compare dictionary sizes or measure splitting.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported detection AUROCs vary by SAE feature. Steering outcomes differ between small and larger amounts.

fits_no_version.finding: Of ten DishonestQA-contrastive SAE features, two detect impostors well out of distribution (AUROC 0.967 and 0.851). Four sit at 0.5, and one is inverse (0.182).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Some SAE features selected on contrastive honesty data generalize to detecting agentic deception, while most do not.

fits_no_version.finding: Steering with the top SAE features left impostor behaviour unchanged at small strength and caused hallucination at large strength.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE-feature steering did not reduce deception in Llama-3.3-70b-instruct impostors in this setting.

record.code_released: The text says the sandbox codebase, game logs, and probe weights are available, but gives no URL.
record.problems: The SAE results give no uncertainty estimates; the SAE model identity is not stated in the relevant section; steering results are qualitative and the tested amounts are not specified.
record.verdict_notes: Relation changed from 'discusses' to 'cites_only': feature splitting is never discussed, and Towards Monosemanticity appears only as a general SAE reference. All rows correctly marked versions ['none']. The 'pretend you're dishonest' probe dataset in the abstract corresponds to DishonestQA/RepEng.

relation.reason: Towards Monosemanticity [40] is cited only as background in Related Work. The paper uses SAEs but not the splitting finding, so uses_without_test would not fit.

tranche.reason: The paper uses Goodfire SAE features for deception detection and steering in Among Us. It never varies dictionary size or measures splitting, families, absorption or objectives.

source_check.notes: Not related to feature splitting. SAE features come from Goodfire's pre-trained SAE for Llama 3.3 70B (ref 24), and Section 4.3 doesn't name the layer. The SAE part is minor: two features detect deception well and steering fails. Shares authors with an original.

statements.problem: None. Table 1 lists ten DishonestQA-contrastive features: 0.967 and 0.851 at the top, four at 0.500, one at 0.182. Steering on Llama-3.3-70b-instruct via Goodfire AutoSteer: normal behaviour at small amounts, hallucination at larger amounts. It leaves out the three moderate features (0.675, 0.638, 0.526), which is an omission, not an error.
